title: Industrial production of spacecraft propellant from extraterrestrial resources

concept.text: The innovation is a durable supply chain that makes spacecraft propellant from resources available beyond Earth and delivers it to vehicles. Its scope extends from obtaining local feedstock and supplying power through chemical processing, storage, transfer and eventual use in flight. The intended capability is routine mission support at useful throughput; demonstrating a chemical reaction establishes only one part of that capability. This system-level definition is a synthesis of the supplied research and review.

Scope clarification: propellant production must be assessed against a vehicle’s actual requirements. Oxygen can serve as an oxidizer, but producing oxygen alone does not supply every component needed by a vehicle that also requires fuel. A plant might replace only part of an Earth-supplied propellant inventory. Its contribution should therefore state which components are locally produced, which remain imported, and whether the stored material can actually be transferred to and used by the intended vehicle.

significance.text: Conditional significance: reliable production near a destination could allow spacecraft to obtain some return or onward propellant there, reducing the amount transported from Earth. This could change mission architecture, potentially freeing launch capacity for payload or enabling additional journeys. The benefit depends on whether the production plant, power system, supporting infrastructure and replacement supplies impose a smaller logistics burden than the propellant they replace.

Further possibilities are conditional on sustained performance: a dependable supply could support repeated surface departures, more flexible exploration schedules or refueling infrastructure serving multiple vehicles. The analogy to terrestrial fuel infrastructure has limits. Resource accessibility, production rate, equipment reliability, maintenance, storage losses and transfer losses determine whether a nominally available resource becomes a useful supply. A successful flight using locally produced material would be an important integration milestone, but would not alone demonstrate durable industrial production.

missing_breakthrough.text: Engineering synthesis: the central missing capability is sustained integration of resource acquisition, power, production, storage and vehicle refueling under extraterrestrial operating conditions. Each stage must deliver material at the quantity, quality and schedule required by the next. A production process can work in isolation while the overall supply chain remains limited by feedstock access, inadequate power, unreliable equipment or losses before flight use.

Concrete engineering questions include how reliably feedstock can be acquired and conditioned; whether production equipment maintains output and product purity over time; and how faults, wear and maintenance are handled with limited human intervention. Storage and transfer must preserve usable inventory and deliver it under the vehicle’s required conditions. Where a chosen propellant requires cryogenic handling, thermal control and fluid management become additional integration challenges. These are proposed engineering considerations, rather than failures established by the supplied source.

The industrial threshold also requires a credible balance between useful output and supporting inputs. Imported equipment and feedstocks, power infrastructure, consumables, spares, maintenance and material losses must be counted. The supplied review identifies this as a coherent system boundary, but its documentary record does not establish which barriers remain unresolved across the field as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a concrete component demonstration to NASA’s MOXIE experiment on Mars: oxygen extraction from atmospheric carbon dioxide on 16 occasions, producing 122 grams in total. These figures are associated with JPL’s September 6, 2023 mission-completion account. However, the supplied source index contains no saved article text, artifacts or hashes, and the review could not independently verify the figures against an inspected passage. They are retained as attributed mission results with that documentary limitation; the absence of captured evidence does not establish that they are false.

The supplied research describes MOXIE as an oxygen-production demonstration that did not produce a complete flight-propellant supply, stockpile flight quantities or refuel a vehicle. Those scope statements likewise remain unverified against captured source text. Taken as described, the result demonstrates one processing step using a local atmospheric resource; it does not establish the integrated storage, transfer, flight use and sustained throughput required by this innovation.

Evidence boundary: the supplied freshness search record is empty, so this record cannot establish developments after the cited 2023 account or the field’s overall status as of November 1, 2026. No additional achieved industrial capability can be inferred from these inputs. This limitation concerns the completeness of the available evidence, rather than showing that subsequent progress did or did not occur.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: an autonomously operated plant on an extraterrestrial body repeatedly obtains local feedstock, produces the declared propellant components, stores them and transfers enough usable material for meaningful ascent or onward journeys. Vehicles should fly using that material. The demonstration should declare its operating duration, throughput, vehicle demand and degree of local sourcing, so that success has a measurable mission context. These are proposed assessment requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated autonomous production of extraterrestrial propellant supports vehicle flight

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility evidence: demonstrate sustained operation over a declared mission-relevant interval and multiple production, storage and transfer cycles. Report output, product quality, inventory losses, interruptions, human interventions, maintenance and recovery from faults. Repeat campaigns and independently assessable measurements would strengthen confidence that performance can recur. A single flight establishes an integrated use case; repeated operation is needed to assess the industrial claim.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained operation across multiple production, storage and transfer cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: disclose imported equipment and feedstocks, the power system, consumables, spares and maintenance requirements, and all relevant production, storage and transfer losses. Compare the resulting logistics burden with a stated alternative that delivers propellant from Earth. Successful operation at one site, with one resource and one vehicle, would establish that demonstrated scope. Finite testing would not establish suitability for every extraterrestrial environment, feedstock, propellant or mission.
completion_criteria.label: Full logistics burden disclosed and compared with Earth-delivered propellant

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AER-01, Mass-access orbital transportation, concerns access to orbit, while AER-03 concerns supplying propellant beyond Earth. They could complement each other, but inexpensive launch does not demonstrate local production, and local production does not establish mass-access launch. AER-02, A probe that returns data from another star system, could share interests in autonomous operation and long-duration reliability; local propellant production alone does not provide the propulsion, navigation or communications needed for an interstellar data-return mission.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-04, Multi-year, near-closed human life support for deep space, overlaps in chemical processing, resource management and sustained reliability. Its defining outcome is maintaining habitable conditions and recycling life-support resources, whereas AER-03 delivers usable propellant to vehicles. AER-05, Economically competitive space-to-Earth solar power, overlaps in power infrastructure, but supplying energy to a propellant plant does not demonstrate economical electricity delivery to Earth.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-06, General-purpose robotic construction of very large space systems, could support assembly or maintenance of production infrastructure. AER-03 does not require or demonstrate general-purpose construction of very large structures. AER-07, An operational defense against civilization-threatening asteroid impacts, could potentially benefit from refueling logistics, but its defining requirements concern detecting threats and executing effective intervention. Propellant production would be an enabling capability in a suitable architecture, not an asteroid-defense demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-08, A space observatory that can test for life on Earth-like exoplanets, might benefit indirectly from transportation or servicing infrastructure; its central advance remains observational capability. AER-09, Sustained, useful air-breathing hypersonic flight, and AER-10, Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion for large, long-range passenger aircraft, share broad propulsion and energy concerns with AER-03. Their defining challenges are atmospheric flight performance and aircraft propulsion, respectively, rather than extraterrestrial resource extraction and spacecraft refueling.

unresolved_issues: The JPL source has no captured text, artifacts or hashes in the supplied record; the MOXIE figures and reported scope limits remain unverified against an inspected passage.
The supplied inputs do not establish subsequent developments or the field’s overall status as of November 1, 2026.
Mission-relevant duration, throughput, acceptable losses, maintenance burden and autonomy requirements remain to be specified for a concrete plant and vehicle.
The resource, location, propellant components and permitted imported feedstocks are unspecified, preventing a quantitative net-logistics assessment.
The completion criteria are proposals without a supplied consensus standard or numerical industrial threshold.

brief.title: Making and delivering rocket propellant beyond Earth
possible: Spacecraft could refuel near their destinations for return trips or onward journeys. Local resources would supply some or all of their propellant—the material a rocket uses for thrust—through a dependable chain of production, storage and delivery.
why: Carrying less propellant from Earth could free launch capacity for cargo or allow additional journeys. A reliable local supply could support repeated departures, more flexible exploration schedules and refueling facilities serving multiple vehicles.

sources.showed: This mission report describes an experiment that extracted oxygen from the atmosphere on Mars.
sources.cited_for: It supports the feasibility of making oxygen from a local resource on Mars.
sources.not_established: Producing oxygen did not establish a complete propellant supply, storage for flight or vehicle refueling.

sources.showed: A demonstration plant produced liquid oxygen and operated automatically across repeated daily cycles. The methane fuel it made was released for analysis.
sources.quote: The system was operated autonomously for four diurnal production cycles
sources.cited_for: It supports automatic operation of a propellant production plant over repeated cycles.
sources.not_established: The demonstration did not establish production beyond Earth, vehicle refueling or flight using its output.

sources.who: Anthony Muscatello, Robert Zubrin, Claire Ohman and Sam Booth
sources.showed: Pioneer Astronautics built a system that converted carbon dioxide and hydrogen into fuel and oxygen. Its output approached a kilogram of combined propellant per day.

sources.cited_for: It supports combining fuel and oxygen production in an integrated processing system.

shown: NASA’s MOXIE experiment extracted oxygen from the atmosphere on Mars, producing 122 grams in total. Oxygen is one component of many rocket propellants; vehicles using it also need fuel. MOXIE did not stockpile enough for flight or refuel a vehicle.

Demonstration plants have also combined fuel and oxygen production and run automatically through repeated cycles. These results establish parts of the supply chain, while the full chain through storage, refueling and repeated flight remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A plant must reliably obtain local resources and turn them into usable propellant with limited human help.
Storage and transfer must preserve enough material, at the required quality, to refuel the intended vehicle.
Repeated flights must use locally produced material supplied through sustained plant operation.
The equipment, power, supplies and maintenance must impose a smaller transport burden than the Earth-delivered propellant they replace.

milestones.label: Repeated automatic production supplies propellant for flight
milestones.explanation: An automatic plant beyond Earth would have to repeatedly obtain local resources, make and store propellant components, and transfer enough for vehicles to fly. This would connect production to useful journeys.

milestones.label: Sustained production, storage and transfer across repeated cycles
milestones.explanation: Repeated cycles would have to sustain output and quality over a mission-relevant period, with losses, maintenance and fault recovery measured. This would establish whether the supply can remain dependable.

milestones.label: Full transport burden compared with delivery from Earth
milestones.explanation: A comparison would have to count imported equipment and materials, power systems, maintenance and losses against delivery from Earth. This would establish the practical benefit for the demonstrated mission.

uncertain: The required operating duration, output, acceptable losses and degree of human assistance depend on the plant and vehicle.
The location, local resource, propellant components and imported materials remain unspecified, so the transport benefit cannot yet be calculated.
There is no agreed numerical threshold here for industrial production; success at one site would not establish suitability elsewhere.

page.title: In-situ propellant production and spacecraft refuelling
page.definition: In-situ propellant production converts local extraterrestrial resources into rocket fuel, oxidizer, or both and supplies them to spacecraft through production, storage and transfer. Oxygen supports fuel combustion as an oxidizer, and cryogenic storage keeps gases liquefied at low temperature.

goal.need: NASA's illustrative four-person Mars ascent budget requires about 32 metric tons of propellant, of which roughly 78% is oxygen. Local oxygen production addresses this Earth-supplied mass while the spacecraft also requires fuel.

figures.caption: NASA's illustrative propellant budget for four people ascending from Mars.
figures.note: Approximate architecture quantities. The total and oxygen fraction in the paragraph are calculated from these masses.

statements.body: NASA, Moon to Mars Objectives, lunar infrastructure objective LI-7.
statements.quote: Demonstrate industrial scale ISRU capabilities in support of continuous human lunar presence and a robust lunar economy.
statements.context: ISRU means in-situ resource utilization, the use of resources available at the destination.

statements.quote: The ultimate aim would be to design a ‘pilot plant’ that could operate sustainably on the Moon
statements.context: ESA's oxygen-extraction programme using lunar regolith, the loose material covering the surface.

statements.body: NASA Space Technology Mission Directorate, lunar ISRU objectives.
statements.quote: Support/promote establishment of reusable/commercial transportation with propellant depots/ISRU propellants

completion.title: An off-Earth plant supplies oxygen through repeated spacecraft refuelling and flight.
completion.criterion: An off-Earth plant produces, cryogenically stores and transfers locally derived oxygen for repeated spacecraft flights at the destination's published production target. Lunar production supplies at least 10 metric tons/year for a nominal 3 years with minimal or no maintenance. Mars production autonomously supplies at least 24 metric tons of liquid oxygen in 16 months preceding crew launch. Delivered oxygen meets the receiving spacecraft's propellant requirements and is used in flight. The mission identifies Earth-supplied fuel and process feedstocks.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, combining destination-specific NASA production targets with ISECG's lunar continuous-refuelling objective.
completion.basis: Searched NASA's Moon to Mars Objectives and ISRU implementation/capability plans, ISECG's ISRU Gap Assessment and ESA's lunar-oxygen material. No published acceptance test combined industrial production, delivery and repeated flight use across destinations. ISECG specifies continuous lunar propellant production, storage and transfer. NASA supplies the destination-specific oxygen targets used here.

milestones.title: Laboratory experiments validate predicted performance of a propellant-production process.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory production of a fuel or oxidizer validates the process's predicted performance, meeting NASA's technology readiness level 3 hardware criterion. Mars evidence includes one Lockheed Martin methane/liquid-oxygen plant reported in 1997 and one Pioneer Astronautics system reported in 2005 that approached 1 kg/day of methane/carbon-monoxide fuel plus oxygen using supplied hydrogen. For lunar feedstocks, ESA reported oxygen extraction from simulant at ESTEC on 17 January 2020 in an agency report without peer review.
milestones.set_by: NASA Earth Science Technology Office, technology readiness level 3 hardware definition.
milestones.threshold_quote: laboratory demonstrations, modeling and simulation validate analytical prediction.

milestones.title: A propellant-production prototype works under its destination's critical environmental conditions.
milestones.criterion: A high-fidelity production prototype addresses critical scaling issues and reproduces predicted performance under relevant environmental conditions, meeting NASA's technology readiness level 6 hardware criterion. A 2026 NASA conference presentation reports one lunar-simulant reactor processing 25 kg under vacuum in late 2024, averaging 0.07 kg/h oxygen during 9 hours of electrolysis. For Mars, NASA's MOXIE archive states that pre-delivery requirements of at least 6 g/h oxygen, greater than 98% purity and at least 10 operating cycles were satisfied.
milestones.set_by: NASA Earth Science Technology Office, technology readiness level 6 hardware definition.

milestones.title: A propellant-production prototype operates in its extraterrestrial environment.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a working production prototype in space, meeting NASA's technology readiness level 7 criterion. One MOXIE instrument produced oxygen from the Martian atmosphere between 20 April 2021 and 7 August 2023. NASA's 6 September 2023 mission report records 16 runs, 122 g total oxygen, and a maximum rate of 12 g/h at at least 98% purity. These mission totals are an agency report without peer review.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Technology Readiness Levels, published on 27 September 2023, level 7.

milestones.title: An off-Earth pilot plant supplies locally made propellant for a vehicle's demonstration flight.
milestones.criterion: An extraterrestrial pilot plant demonstrates the complete chain from resource acquisition through propellant production, liquefaction, storage and transfer, and an uncrewed ascent vehicle or hopper uses its product in a demonstration flight. NASA's implementation plan specifies initial use in a non-mission-critical application. ISECG separately requires demonstration of liquefaction, storage and transfer before sustained operations.
milestones.set_by: NASA's 2022 ISRU implementation plan, slides 6–7, and ISECG's 2021 Gap Assessment, Table 5b, objective 4. These criteria were written for lunar demonstrations with Mars applications.
milestones.threshold_quote: Initially use ISRU-derived commodity in non-mission critical application

milestones.title: An off-Earth plant makes 10 metric tons of oxygen/year on the Moon or 24 metric tons in 16 months on Mars.
milestones.criterion: Meet NASA's destination-specific oxygen-production targets. Lunar regolith processing supplies at least 10 metric tons of oxygen/year for a nominal 3 years with minimal or no maintenance. A Mars plant autonomously produces at least 24 metric tons of liquid oxygen in the 16 months preceding launch of the human crew. This milestone establishes production of the mission-scale inventory.
milestones.set_by: NASA STMD, Envisioned Future Priorities, slide 13, for lunar regolith oxygen. NASA Planetary Data System's MOXIE description supplies the human-Mars architecture target.
milestones.threshold_quote: minimum of 10 mT O2/yr; 3 years nom. with min./no maintenance

not_found: No numerical operating-lifetime or lander-capacity specification was found for ISECG's continuous-refuelling objective.
No primary result was located for lunar in-situ propellant production, an extraterrestrial pilot refuelling flight, or either destination's full-scale production target.
The full 1997 ISRU proceedings, ESA's 2019 Space Resources Strategy and the 2022 MOXIE Science Advances article could not be opened.
